strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: active perception is cast as a POMDP where the reward combines a differentiable prediction loss with an action-regularization term, and the gradient decomposition into a policy gradient plus a supervised prediction-loss gradient (Eq. 3) is derived cleanly and made fully transparent in the appendix.

Thorough empirical study: five benchmarks spanning classification (MHSB, CircleSquare, TactileMNIST), regression (TactileMNISTVolume), and pose estimation (Toolbox), run with 5 seeds each, extensive HEBO hyperparameter tuning, and additional ablations (APPLE-RND, APPLE-PPO, APPLE-PPO-LSTM) that credibly isolate the contribution of off-policy learning from architecture choices.

Honest and insightful analysis: the authors openly report that the random baseline solves the MHSB task (exposing a limitation of prior work HAM), that APPLE-SAC fails on the Toolbox task without tuning, and that their methods are sample-hungry (up to 5-10M steps), rather than overclaiming.
Reproducibility is taken seriously: full hyperparameter tables, hardware and implementation details (replay buffer design, JIT-compiled training loop), and a promise of open-source code.
Useful practical finding that CrossQ-based variant is more robust to hyperparameter transfer across tasks and roughly halves training time compared to the SAC variant.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core approach is a fairly direct combination of existing components (SAC/CrossQ + ViViT-style transformer backbone applied to glimpse-based perception, in the spirit of RAM (Mnih et al., 2014) and HAM); the conceptual contribution beyond swapping on-policy for off-policy RL is modest.

Simulation-only evaluation: despite the strong robotics motivation and claims about advancing active perception in robotics, there are no real-robot experiments; the tactile tasks rely on a simulated GelSight (Taxim) sensor, so sim-to-real validity is untested.

Weak baselines on the harder tasks: for the regression and localization tasks the only baseline is a random policy; recent learned active-tactile-perception methods (e.g., ActExplore, Niemann et al. 2024, Tandem) are discussed but not compared, weakening the 'general framework' claim.

Marginal and noisy gains on regression: on TactileMNISTVolume the improvement over the random baseline (e.g., final error 0.99 vs 1.07 cm3) is small relative to the seed variance, and no statistical significance testing is reported.

Generality claims are stronger than the evidence: all tasks use the same sensor modality, similar action spaces, and largely the same benchmark suite (Schneider et al., 2025); cross-modality or cross-domain transfer, which would substantiate 'general active perception', is left to future work.

Sample efficiency is poor (millions of environment steps, 40-50 GPU-hours per run), which limits practical significance and is only acknowledged, not addressed (e.g., no pre-training or representation-learning ablation).

strengths: The empirical evaluation is relatively thorough for this domain: five benchmarks spanning classification and regression, 5 seeds per method, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization with details of the search space and procedure, and ablations (APPLE-PPO/APPLE-PPO-LSTM, longer HAM training runs) that strengthen the comparison against prior work.

The paper makes a useful observation that the MHSB task used to validate HAM is nearly trivially solvable due to a small discretized observation space, and provides honest reporting of baselines (APPLE-RND) that expose where active perception is and is not actually needed.

The formalization of active perception as a POMDP with a decomposed action space and a differentiable prediction-loss reward is clearly presented, with the derivation of the decomposed gradient (policy gradient + supervised loss gradient) provided in the appendix.
Reproducibility is taken seriously: full hyperparameter tables, hardware details, replay-buffer design, and a statement that the codebase will be released.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty. The core idea—jointly training a glimpse-selection policy and a predictor with a reward equal to negative prediction loss—is essentially RAM (Mnih et al., 2014) and its tactile adaptation HAM (Fleer et al., 2020). The main new ingredient is swapping REINFORCE/PPO for off-policy SAC/CrossQ and an LSTM for a transformer. The claimed contribution of 'a general framework' is a straightforward re-combination of existing components, and the theory (Eq. 2–3) is a direct application of the policy gradient theorem to a modified reward.

The generality claim is overclaimed relative to the evidence. All experiments use tasks from a single benchmark suite (TactileMNIST) in the same simulator family, a single sensor modality, and a fixed episode structure. 'General active perception' is not demonstrated across modalities, environments, or sim-to-real; no real-robot experiments are included despite the motivation being robotic manipulation.

Missing comparisons to relevant recent RL-based active perception methods. The paper cites ActExplore (Shahidzadeh et al., 2024), Niemann et al. (2024), and Xu et al. (2022) but empirically compares only against HAM (2020) and a random-action baseline. Without these baselines, it is unclear whether APPLE advances the state of the art or merely catches up with standard off-policy RL.

Results on the regression tasks are weak and unconvincing: on TactileMNISTVolume the improvements over the random baseline are small (~1.1 vs ~1.28 cm³) with large variance across seeds, and APPLE-SAC fails on the Toolbox task without task-specific tuning—undercutting the central claim of task-agnostic generality.

The comparison to HAM is confounded: HAM's reward is modified to the negative prediction loss (departing from its original formulation), and its architecture (LSTM) differs from APPLE's transformer, so it is hard to attribute HAM's failures to on-policy RL rather than to the architecture or the reward change, despite the attempt via APPLE-PPO-LSTM.

Sample efficiency and cost are significant practical drawbacks (up to 5M–10M environment steps, 40–50 hours per run on a dedicated GPU), acknowledged in the limitations but not resolved; the framing 'toward general active perception' promises more than the delivered scope.

Minor issues: the CrossQ citation is inaccurate (dated 2019; the method paper is from 2022), and the assumption that predictions y_t do not influence the environment (justifying Eq. 2) deserves more discussion since the physical actions used to gather information are entangled with the prediction outputs in the same network.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: active perception is framed as a POMDP where predictions are part of the action space, and the objective cleanly decomposes into a policy gradient plus a supervised prediction-loss gradient (Eq. 3), providing a principled unified optimization.

Genuinely general design: the same framework (shared transformer backbone, joint policy + perception training) is applied unchanged across classification (CircleSquare, TactileMNIST, MHSB) and regression (volume estimation, pose estimation) tasks with different observation spaces.

Careful and honest experimental methodology: 5 seeds per method, models trained from scratch, hyperparameters tuned via HEBO on representative tasks and reused without per-task tuning to test robustness, and evaluation on held-out objects/configurations.

The inclusion of a random-policy baseline (APPLE-RND) is very informative — it exposes that the MHSB task is nearly solvable by memorization (1,681 distinct observations per class), which is a valuable community contribution that critically contextualizes prior work (HAM).

Additional PPO-based ablations (APPLE-PPO, APPLE-PPO-LSTM) cleanly isolate the on-policy vs. off-policy and LSTM vs. transformer factors behind HAM's failure, supporting the central design claims with evidence rather than assertion.

Good qualitative analysis (Fig. 14 showing a learned circular search pattern and disambiguation behavior), detailed implementation/hyperparameter appendices, reproducibility statement with open-source code commitment, and a candid limitations section (sample inefficiency of up to 5–10M steps, simulation-only, single sensor).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core contribution is essentially adapting SAC/CrossQ to a POMDP setting with a supervised loss term added to the reward and a transformer history encoder. Each component (off-policy RL for partially observed control, joint actor-critic representation learning) is well established; the derivation in Eq. 3 is straightforward and the adaptation items (trajectory inputs, dynamic reward recomputation, augmented policy gradient) are fairly mechanical.

All experiments are in simulation; despite the strong robotics motivation (tactile exploration of cluttered environments), there is no real-robot validation, and the tasks — MNIST-style digits, a toy CircleSquare, one wrench — remain far simpler than the motivating scenarios, so the claim of a 'general framework for advancing active perception in robotics' is not yet empirically supported.

Baseline coverage is thin: beyond HAM (which fails or degenerates on most tasks) and the authors' own random baseline, there is no comparison against other plausible general approaches (e.g., model-based exploration, Bayesian optimization / information-gain methods on the same tasks, or other off-policy POMDP RL variants such as R2D2-style or Dreamer-style agents).

Robustness claims are undermined by APPLE-SAC's failure on the Toolbox task without per-task tuning; only APPLE-CrossQ transfers, and the authors themselves admit that 'more experiments are needed' to substantiate the robustness hypothesis.

The sample efficiency problem is severe and only acknowledged, not addressed: 5–10M environment steps (40–50 hours per run on a dedicated GPU) for tasks with 32×32 tactile images makes real-world applicability questionable, and no experiments with pre-trained encoders are provided despite this being proposed as a remedy.

Ablations on the architecture are incomplete: embedding sharing across Q-networks and policy is claimed to work better 'empirically' but no ablation table is shown; likewise there is limited analysis of what exploration strategies are actually learned on the tactile tasks (only one qualitative Toolbox example).

The comparison against HAM uses a modified reward (negative prediction loss instead of the original 0-1 reward); while the authors argue this is fairer, it means the HAM numbers are not directly comparable to the original publication and the reproduction differences are only briefly addressed.

strengths: Clear unified formulation of active perception as a POMDP with a decomposable objective (policy gradient + supervised prediction loss), requiring only a differentiable loss and ground-truth labels — a clean and well-motivated generalization of joint perception-action learning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five benchmarks (classification, regression, pose estimation) spanning different observation spaces, with 5 seeds per method and metrics computed on held-out objects/images.

Thoughtful and honest baseline analysis: the paper does not just beat HAM but provides a convincing diagnosis (the MHSB task is nearly solvable by memorization with random touches, and the APPLE-RND baseline confirms this), which is a genuine contribution to understanding prior work.

Extensive ablations in the appendix (LSTM vs. transformer, pure-RL vs. supervised loss, grid-search vs. learned policy, sparse rewards, PPO variants, HAM with modified reward) that support the design choices and the claim that off-policy methods are better suited to active perception than on-policy ones.

Good robustness analysis: APPLE-CrossQ transfers hyperparameters across tasks without retuning and reduces training time ~53%, and emergent exploration behaviors are qualitatively analyzed (Figs. 8, 12).
Detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameter tables, HEBO tuning procedure, hardware, buffer design) and transparent LLM-usage disclosure.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core idea (jointly learning a glimpse-selection policy and a prediction head with REINFORCE) originates from RAM (Mnih et al., 2014) and HAM (Fleer et al., 2020); the main delta is swapping in off-policy RL (SAC/CrossQ) and a transformer backbone, which is a straightforward substitution rather than a new algorithmic insight. The theoretical derivation (Eq. 3) is standard.

All experiments are in simulation on relatively simple or toy tasks (CircleSquare is a 2-class toy problem); no real-robot experiments despite the paper being framed for robotics, which weakens the central claim of generality for active perception.

Severe sample inefficiency (up to 5–10M steps per task, 40–50 GPU-hours per run), acknowledged by the authors but leaving practical applicability open; the proposed remedies (pre-training, better RL) are only sketched.

Baseline coverage is thin: apart from HAM, no comparison to other recent RL-based active perception methods (e.g., Xu et al. 2022, Niemann et al. 2024, Shahidzadeh et al. 2024, or baselines from the Tactile MNIST benchmark suite it builds on), so it is unclear whether the tasks are 'solved' relative to what other methods could achieve.

Results on the regression tasks are comparatively weak and high-variance: e.g., on TactileMNISTVolume the final-error gap between APPLE variants and the random baseline is small (~0.08–0.09 cm³), and on Toolbox APPLE-SAC fails, which somewhat undercuts the 'general across tasks' claim; no definitive explanation or fix is offered.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: 'comprehensive empirical evaluation' and 'versatile and general framework' rest on five simulated tasks, mostly sharing the same simulator, sensor model, and action structure; scalability to multi-fingered/multi-modal settings is left as future work.
The TactileMNISTVolume comparison is confounded by the fact that hyperparameters were tuned only on classification tasks, making the regression comparison between methods partly unfair/uninformative.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and well-motivated problem formulation, framing active perception as a POMDP where the gradient of the objective decomposes into a policy-gradient term and a supervised prediction-loss term; the derivation (Eq. 1-3 and Appendix G) is straightforward but clearly written.

The empirical evaluation is comparatively thorough for this area: five benchmarks spanning classification, regression, and pose estimation; 5 seeds per run; hyperparameters tuned with a Bayesian optimizer (HEBO); an off-policy (SAC/CrossQ) vs. on-policy (REINFORCE/PPO/HAM) comparison; and multiple ablations (LSTM vs. transformer backbone, pure-RL vs. supervised loss, grid-search policy, sparse rewards, and a downstream-task variant).

The analysis is unusually honest in places: the authors themselves show that the MHSB task used to evaluate HAM is nearly solvable by a random policy, and they reproduce HAM on its original task to validate their implementation before claiming it fails on harder tasks.

The finding that off-policy methods (especially CrossQ) are substantially more sample-efficient and more robust to hyperparameter transfer than on-policy methods for active perception is a useful, practically relevant insight.

Reasonable reproducibility: implementation details (JAX/Flax, replay buffer sizing, hardware, wall-clock times), hyperparameter tables, and an explicit statement that no code release appears to be planned... though see weaknesses.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea — jointly training an attention/recurrent perception module with a policy-gradient action head for glimpse selection — is essentially RAM (Mnih et al., 2014) and HAM (Fleer et al., 2020) with SAC/CrossQ substituted for REINFORCE and a transformer substituted for an LSTM. The theoretical contribution (gradient decomposition) is a straightforward consequence of the reward structure, and the architectural choices (ViT + ViViT-style backbone) are standard. The paper's own framing ('a step towards a more general framework') implicitly concedes this.

Generality claims are stronger than the evidence. The central selling point is a task-agnostic framework, but all experiments are in simulation with a narrow action space (2D sensor translation), a single sensor modality per task, and mostly small/toy problems (28x28 glimpses, MNIST digits, one wrench). There is no real-robot evaluation, no cross-task policy transfer, and no multi-modal or multi-finger experiment — the regimes where generality would actually be tested. The claim that 'no active perception method has been shown to work on a wide range of tasks' is a framing device rather than a demonstrated capability of APPLE.

The external baseline coverage is thin: HAM is the only learned baseline besides the authors' own variants (random policy, PPO ablation). Recent RL-based active tactile perception methods (e.g., Xu et al. 2022 'Tandem', Shahidzadeh et al. 2024 'ActExplore', Niemann et al. 2024) are discussed in related work but not compared against, even on the shared TactileMNIST benchmark, which weakens the empirical claims.

Severe sample inefficiency is acknowledged but unresolved: up to 5-10M environment steps and 40-50 GPU-hours per run for tasks as simple as classifying MNIST digits or a circle vs. square. This severely limits practical significance for robotics, and the sim-to-real discussion remains speculative.

On the MHSB task the random baseline reaches ~100%, so that comparison is uninformative about learned exploration; the meaningful HAM comparison rests on CircleSquare, where HAM fails entirely after 10M steps — a result that mostly demonstrates HAM's limitations rather than a positive capability of APPLE on a hard problem.

Performance on the more realistic regression/localization tasks is mixed and not clearly above baselines: on TactileMNISTVolume all methods are within noise of each other (final errors 0.99-1.07 cm^3), and APPLE-SAC fails on the Toolbox task unless tuned; only one of the two proposed variants works consistently.
No code release is mentioned; combined with the heavy reliance on hyperparameter search, reproducibility of the full result set is uncertain.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated unified formulation of active perception as a POMDP with a combined RL + supervised objective; the derivation showing the gradient decomposes into a policy gradient and a prediction-loss gradient is clean and correctly presented.

Substantial and honest empirical work: five benchmarks spanning classification, regression, and pose estimation; 5 seeds per method; hyperparameters tuned with a Bayesian optimizer (HEBO); multiple ablations (LSTM vs. transformer, pure-RL vs. supervised loss, grid-search policy, sparse rewards, a downstream-task variant).

Particularly valuable critical analysis of prior work: the paper shows the MHSB task used by HAM is nearly solvable by memorization (only 1,681 distinct observations per class), which meaningfully recontextualizes earlier claims, and validates its own HAM reproduction with a longer run (Fig. 20).

The PPO vs. SAC/CrossQ comparison (Fig. 14) provides genuine insight into why off-policy methods suit active perception, and the CrossQ variant's robustness across tasks without retuning plus the 53% training-time reduction is a practical, useful finding.

Well-organized paper with good figures of learned behaviors, thorough appendices (hyperparameters, implementation details, derivations, limitations), and a reproducibility statement; limitations (sample efficiency, simulation-only, single sensor) are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially off-policy RL (SAC/CrossQ) with a supervised loss added to the reward and shared transformer backbone — a fairly direct extension of RAM/HAM (Mnih et al. 2014; Fleer et al. 2020) with modern components. The mathematical derivation is straightforward and the core idea could be summarized in a sentence.

The claimed 'generality' is not demonstrated by transfer: the agent is retrained from scratch per task, hyperparameters still need per-task-family tuning, and all main tasks come from a single benchmark suite (TactileMNIST, Schneider et al. 2025), which appears connected to the authors (shared co-authors with the benchmark). Generality claims should be tempered.

Entirely simulation-only: no real-robot experiments despite the paper's positioning toward robotics; the authors acknowledge sim-to-real for vision-based tactile sensors is very challenging, leaving practical significance unproven.

Sample inefficiency is severe (up to 5–10M environment steps, ~40–50 GPU-hours per run), which the paper acknowledges; this limits real-world applicability and weakens the argument over on-policy baselines, which are at least wall-clock faster (4x).

Baselines are relatively weak and dated: the main learned baseline (HAM, 2020) fails on new tasks, and beyond the random policy there is no comparison to more recent active-perception RL approaches (e.g., PPO-based methods of Xu et al. 2022, Shahidzadeh et al. 2024) on the same benchmarks.

Some evaluation details raise questions: metrics on CircleSquare/MHSB are computed on 'unseen objects' but these tasks have only two or four objects, so generalization is trivially easy there; the volume-estimation improvements over the random baseline are modest (~0.1 cm³) with large variance.
